title: Finally, ADHD Has A Published accelerated TMS Trial
subtitle: Brain medicine research success!
body_html:
There are some hit makers who just keep cranking out hits. I think of the Beatles, Motown, and, of course, Dr. Linda Carpenter.

For those who aren't familiar with Dr. Carpenter, she is faculty at Brown University, and has been a crucial early adopter of Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation, and is a principal investigator on a study of Prism fMRI-EEG biomarker neurofeedback for depression that is recruiting now, as well as the principal investigator and first author on the ProlivRx pivotal trial, called the MOOD study. She's a scientist so prolific her work led to a job for me. (I’m CMO at Neurolief, which makes ProlivRx, an at-home adjunctive treatment for depression).

And this past week, Dr. Carpenter senior authored a paper in Brain Stimulation that everyone's been waiting for on ADHD treated with TMS—specifically, the intermittent Theta Burst Stimulation (iTBS) pattern developed in neurophysiology labs and then pioneered for clinical care in the THREE-D trial by Dr. Jonathan Downar. Later, Eli Cole and Nolan Williams would use it in SAINT TMS, and Colleen Hanlon, Aron Tendler, and I would use it in SWIFT TMS. Let’s shift back to Dr. Carpenter!

Specifically, she and coauthors enrolled 34 adolescents between 12 and 18 years old in a double blind sham controlled crossover trial looking at iTBS in the treatment of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder in kids with parent-reported working memory deficits.

The stimulation use the same LDLPFC anatomic site as traditional TMS for depression, with the same figure-8 coil that's available in many doctor’s offices, and stimulated with just 600 pulses in about 3 minutes per session. Participants received 10 once-daily iTBS sessions and 10 once-daily sham sessions. There were details in the supplemental materials:

Participants completed two phases, with iTBS administered during the first 10 visits of each phase. Symptom status was gathered before the first iTBS session, immediately before the 6th iTBS session, and ~24 hours after the last session. A washout between phases was 6 weeks, except for one participant who waited four weeks due to sports season conflict.1

Yes, friends, when you're designing clinical trials for adolescents, you need to take sports season into account or you are not gonna enroll anybody.

Although they used anatomical landmarks instead of functional connectivity, the study was done with concurrent EEG and MRI guidance:

All participants wore a neoprene EEG cap (64 electrodes) during resting Motor Threshold (rMT) and iTBS treatment procedures for consistency across sessions (as some visits involved EEG recording). The Nexstim device models the induced E-field maximum (V/m) value on the cortical surface based on the individual participant's anatomical MRI data and the physics of the coil.

I mentioned the details of the method section from the supplemental materials not because I want to bore you. I get that it's a research lab, and they're doing fancy research stuff. Dr. Carpenter also provides clinical care in her center, and I'm noting all this for you because I think it's evidence of my brain medicine is here thesis. I've been advancing it in this very newsletter, and in my work at Radial.

This is a lab that not only can do TMS, but it can also incorporate MRI data, and it can simultaneously collect EEG data too. All of these tools are becoming a standard part of Brain Medicine care. This kind of care, when it's deployed as Dr. Carpenter does, will require multiple disciplines working together, and it will enabled by AI.

And what were the results? It worked.

…statistically significant difference in symptom change across time was identified between the treatment conditions in parent-reported WM [working memory] symptoms (p = .025; d = −.58), with statistically significant condition differences after 10 sessions (p < .05; Fig. 1A-B).

Among secondary outcome measures, a statistically significant condition x time difference was identified for change in parent-reported a) overall ADHD symptoms (p = .037; d = −.48),

b) anger (p = .01; d = −.87),

c) depressive symptoms (p = .007; d = −.62), and

d) anxiety symptoms (p < .001; d = −.98).

What's special notable about these outcomes? They are statistically significant even in a very small sample size. That suggests that the difference that Dr. Carpenter has detected is actually a very large one—anything you can see clearly in a small sample is more likely to be a big difference at scale, if it replicates.

Of note, this is the third randomized control trial demonstrating TMS is effective in pediatric ADHD, but it's the first using the more brief iTBS stimulation at only 80% threshold, a relatively low dose of energy delivered.

They even added an additional open-label accelerated iTBS follow up after the study, and that seems to be plausible as a treatment approach as well:

Further, in an open-label trial of twice-daily iTBS (3600 pulses per day) for 5 or 10 days to previously enrolled participants in the clinical trial, twice-daily iTBS was safe, feasible, tolerated, and effective for acutely improving parent-reported ADHD, working memory, and mood symptoms. Given the rapidly growing literature on safety and efficacy of protocols that administer numerous iTBS sessions per day [6], accelerated may iTBS will may show improved feasibility and comparable efficacy to traditional once per day iTBS for ADHD.

We will, of course, need to replicate these findings, and more work will be done before there's an FDA label from somebody. But it's coming—obviously. Then our friends at healthcare payors we need to hear the clamor from all of us, as they have already heard for accelerated TMS generally. As a brief note, in the past couple of weeks, we've gotten accelerated transcranial magnetic stimulation coverage policies in place for a mix of either or both SAINT and SWIFT protocols in Blue Cross Blue Shield plans from California to Texas to South Carolina. These follow Highmark BCBS, Premera BCBS, CareFirst BCBS, and probably more plans with progressive policies—a nationwide standard of medical necessity is being set in the treatment of depression, and it's likely that PTSD, bipolar, depression, OCD, and even ADHD might be next. It may be that the days of highly restrictive coverage policies, I'm looking at you other payors—might also need to be updated!

Thank you for reading! I hope to see you all at the rapid acting mental health treatment event in San Francisco on May 16. If you're reading this, you get to use the code “FREE” to get a free ticket.
